channel.description: The open inner monologue of Nicolás Baglivo.

item.title: Reaccion
item.content:encoded: El otro día estaba leyendo el blog de Lole, su idea de escribir para tender puentes resonó profundamente, pero algo me dice que los puentes no se tienden sino que ya existen. Para mí la escritura no es trasladar afuera lo que está adentro, a veces pienso que mi cerebro ni siquiera está involucrado en el proceso, son mis manos las que directamente solidifican algo que hay flotando en el aire, algo que ya existe, que emerge de todo lo que está pasando. Mis manos son meras herramientas que materializan en letras algo que ya existe. El contraste con la idea de Lole es que no hay un origen y un puente que se tiende hacia un destino, un receptor, lo que hay es una sensación que se manifiesta en palabras, algo que ya estaba y que ya nos conectaba, como el aire invisible, y que ha tomado una forma donde nuestra consciencia puede entenderla. Por eso creo que es normal sentir que ya sabías algo cuando lo leés, sentir que ya conocías a esta persona que lo escribe, a veces incluso sentir que lo podrías haber escrito vos. Escribir es transformar algo que percibimos que habita en otro universo y hacerlo visible en el nuestro. Y por qué lo hacemos? Porque no tenemos opción, pero nos alegramos cuando sucede, porque nuestro instinto es que hay algo más, algo que nos conecta, el puente siempre estuvo ahí, ahora lo vemos.

item.title: Notes to self
item.content:encoded:
Things I'd like to make sure I don't forget.

  1. Frustration is natural, endure discomfort, it is inevitable and manageable.
  2. Everything has a trade-off. Understand the risks you're choosing.
  3. We move forward by doing. Avoid overthinking. Use intuition. Act small.
  4. Don't take things so seriously.
  5. Feel connection and excitement with your work — chase that feeling.
  6. When the body wanders, the mind follows — walks invite creativity.
  7. Motivation appears while doing, not before.
  8. Step away — time and distance often finish the thought.
  9. Craft with care and authenticity.

item.title: On Authenticity
item.content:encoded: I've been reading the book Tiny Experiments, haven't finished it yet but it really fits the way I think about things and adds up to something I have been thinking lately which is things you accept even tho you don't believe in them. I have been repeating that thinking of outcomes is the most important thing, trying to find metrics to know where we are, I have used SMART to work with people to achieve their goals... all because I thought that's what a good leader does, that's how I have been taught good leaders operate, and probably many do, with good results, but that does not mean that it has to work for me and certainly does not mean it is the only way, so why did I disregard my own instinct and follow this way of working? And why was I surprised when they did not yield the best results? I was simply trying to fit. I have learned to speak my mind over the years, I have gained confidence while doing it, but I have also compromised where I shouldn't have, I have also worked in ways that I did not believe in, and I'm not saying I'm always right or that everything should work my way, but when you know, you know, there's a very particular feeling I have when I'm doing something that compromises my authenticity which is very different from what I feel when I'm simply doing something that I just think won't work or that is stupid. I'm fine with experimenting with things that I believe don't have a good chance to succeed, especially when I believe in the person proposing this, but I'm not okay anymore with feeling I'm compromising on who I am, I'm done trying to fit.

item.title: I told you so
item.content:encoded: I hate to be the I-told-you-so person, but I ended up in that position way too many times. Because I hated to be that person, I did not do it; I just accepted that it was time to change and help to drive that change. My way to not be that I-told-you-so person was to never say I told you so, but I always still felt bad about that. I knew I could have done something more — that I wasn't being true to my gut. Not because I chose to not mourn the loss and focus on the future, that was the right part, but because I let the thing happen in the first place. To be the I-told-you-so person, you need to be the "I let that happen" person first. Today I still hate to be the "I told you so" person, but I try to avoid it by working on preventing the situation from happening, by being vocal about my thoughts, by gathering data to support it, and by pushing as hard as I think I need to, to make sure my point is made.

item.title: Learning not to burn out
item.content:encoded:
I was spiraling, in german they call this "Teufelskreis", when you just can´t stop thinking how bad things are, and with every thought you just reaffirm all that despair, it just becomes worse and worse. I grew as a person during that process.

As you can imagine, things were bad. The organisation was doing everything wrong and there was nothing I could do about it, I tried of course, I explained, I warned, I complained, I screamed. Nobody listened, and I felt powerless, I could see the end of the story and it wasn´t good, and the worst part was that there was nothing I could do about it.

Sounds like a horrible drama movie, it wasn´t, it was just work. But for someone whose work has been a big part of my life, who used work as a way to avoid other things in life, this was a big deal, this mattered and things were going to hell.

Of course things were not that bad, and not everything was wrong, in fact, things are rarely just right or wrong, at the end of the day it is just opinions and results — and being responsible for them.

My way out of this "Teufelskreis" was learning something simple: work is work. Nobody dies, at least in my line of work. Nothing is purely right or wrong, and everyone is just trying to do their best.

So if you don't agree with something, don't despair. Be true to your thoughts, be authentic, be loud and courageous. And if things still don't go the way you want them to, let them go.

And if by letting them go, the workplace becomes a place where you no longer feel like you can be you and do what you think needs to be done, at least to some meaningful extent, then move on to the next thing. That's what I did. This has been a valuable lesson in life, not just for work, but for everything, and I'm grateful.

If you are going through a similar experience and you want to talk about it, I´m here to listen. You can reach out to me at hi@nbaglivo.dev.
